tagline: Nine interstate miles combine mountain views with crossings for wildlife.
intro: The Interstate 26 Scenic Highway crosses Appalachian mountain terrain in Madison County, running nine miles from Exit 9 near Mars Hill to the Tennessee line. North Carolina DOT presents this designated byway as a combination of mountain views, engineering and environmental features, with a drive time of ten minutes. Two scenic overlooks punctuate the highway, and the climb reaches Buckner Gap before the road approaches the state line.

I-26 originally ended at Asheville; its northward extension into Tennessee followed between 2003 and 2005. The Madison County section opened in late 2003. Wildlife received crossings of its own: two concrete passages beneath the highway allow bears, deer and other animals to cross without entering traffic. Each culvert measures eight feet by eight feet.

Although the signs say west, this part of I-26 runs toward the north; the route’s signed directions follow interstate numbering conventions. Follow signed I-26 West from Exit 9 toward Tennessee, passing the first overlook just beyond the interchange. The route climbs to Buckner Gap, crosses the Laurel River near Wolf Laurel and approaches Sams Gap. At the state line, the Appalachian Trail passes beneath the highway through an underpass, with a small parking lot built for hikers.

moments.title: First scenic overlook
moments.text: The first overlook west of Exit 9 puts two very different roads in the same view: I-26 and the Blue Ridge Parkway across the valley. Below the highway is California Creek Church. The white frame church was built in 1917 and moved to its present location in 1937. Its design combines Gothic Revival form with Colonial Revival decoration, including paired entrances in corner towers. Another crossing nearby is concealed from interstate travelers: one of the highway’s two wildlife passages. The concrete culverts give bears, deer and other wildlife a way through the corridor beneath the traffic.
moments.notice: Look across the valley for the Blue Ridge Parkway and below the highway for California Creek Church.

moments.title: Buckner Gap
moments.text: The highway climbs to its high point at Buckner Gap. Near the top, North Carolina DOT created one of its first monarch butterfly sanctuaries to enhance roadside habitat. It is difficult to see from the highway. The route also has three runaway truck ramps on the eastbound side.

moments.title: Laurel River bridge
moments.text: Near Wolf Laurel, the bridge carries I-26 across the Laurel River with an automatic de-icing system built into its design. Completed in 2002, the bridge stands in mountain country subject to heavy snow and icing. When the system detects icing, it sprays liquid onto the bridge deck. North Carolina DOT identifies the nozzles along the bridge’s sides as a visible part of that system. Beyond the bridge, the road approaches Sams Gap and the Tennessee boundary, where another kind of traveler crosses underneath: the Appalachian Trail runs through an underpass at the state line.
moments.notice: The spray nozzles along the bridge’s sides belong to its automatic de-icing system.
